items: ᚠ · sound "f" · Freyr's ætt · name means cattle, wealth
resources, earned value, generosity, flow

The name comes from the Proto-Germanic word for cattle, which for early farming peoples was wealth that could walk. All three rune poems, the Old Norwegian, the Old Icelandic and the Anglo-Saxon, begin with it: the Norse verses warn that riches stir up quarrels among kin, while the Anglo-Saxon poem calls wealth a comfort to everyone, though anyone who hopes for honor before the Lord should share it freely.
ᚢ · sound "u" · Freyr's ætt · name means aurochs, the great wild ox
strength, vitality, endurance, untamed energy

The name is usually reconstructed as the word for the aurochs, the huge wild ox of European forests that died out in the 1600s. All three rune poems cover it, but in different ways: the Anglo-Saxon poem describes the fierce, great-horned aurochs, the Old Norwegian reads its name as slag from poor iron, and the Old Icelandic as drizzling rain.
ᚦ · sound "th" · Freyr's ætt · name means giant (the Anglo-Saxon name means thorn)
protection, resistance, a sharp edge, pausing before acting

The Old Norwegian and Old Icelandic poems call it þurs, a giant, one of the wild forces that trouble an ordered life, while the Anglo-Saxon poem names it þorn, a thorn that is cruel to anyone who grabs it. The rune lived on as the letter þ (thorn), which Icelandic still uses today.
ᚨ · sound "a" · Freyr's ætt · name means a god, one of the Æsir
communication, insight, inspiration, listening

Its name meant one of the Æsir, the gods, and modern readers link it above all with Odin, the god of poetry and hard-won wisdom. All three rune poems cover it but hear the name differently: the Old Icelandic poem as a god, the Old Norwegian as the mouth of a river, and the Anglo-Saxon as the mouth from which all speech begins.
ᚱ · sound "r" · Freyr's ætt · name means riding, a journey
journey, rhythm, direction, timing

The name means riding or a journey. All three rune poems cover it; the Anglo-Saxon one notes with some humor that riding seems easy to anyone sitting indoors and hard for the one covering the long miles, and both Norse poems spare a thought for the horse that does the work.
ᚲ · sound "k" · Freyr's ætt · name means torch (the Norse poems' name means a sore)
clarity, craft, creativity, learning

Its old name is uncertain. The Anglo-Saxon poem calls it cēn, a torch burning brightly where people rest indoors, while both Norse poems call it kaun, a sore or ulcer. The name Kenaz is a modern reconstruction built on the torch.
ᚷ · sound "g" · Freyr's ætt · name means gift
gift, exchange, partnership, balance

Gebo means gift. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem covers it, praising generosity as an honor to the giver and a lifeline to those who have nothing. In early Germanic custom a gift was never quite free: it created a tie and called for something in return.
ᚹ · sound "w" · Freyr's ætt · name means joy
joy, belonging, contentment, harmony

The name means joy. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem covers it, describing the joy of someone who knows little sorrow and has enough for a good home. The rune also lived on as the letter wynn (ƿ), which scribes used for the w sound in Old English manuscripts.
ᚺ · sound "h" · Heimdall's ætt · name means hail
disruption, release, forces beyond control, transformation

Hagalaz means hail, and the second ætt is often called Hagal's ætt after it. All three rune poems cover it and picture hail as a kind of grain: the coldest grain in the Norse verses, the whitest in the Anglo-Saxon poem, which adds that it whirls down from the sky and turns to water. That turn, from hard grain to water the ground can drink, shapes most modern readings.
ᚾ · sound "n" · Heimdall's ætt · name means need, necessity
need, constraint, patience, resourcefulness

The name means need or necessity. All three rune poems cover it; the Norse verses picture hardship that leaves little room to choose, while the Anglo-Saxon poem observes that need tightens the heart yet often turns into help when it is attended to early.
ᛁ · sound "i" · Heimdall's ætt · name means ice
stillness, pause, clarity, waiting

The name means ice. All three rune poems cover it: the Anglo-Saxon poem dwells on ice gleaming like glass and treacherously slippery, the Old Norwegian calls it a broad bridge, and the Old Icelandic a roof over the water.
ᛃ · sound "j (as y in yes)" · Heimdall's ætt · name means year, a good harvest
harvest, cycles, patience, reward for effort

The name means year, in the sense of a good season and the crops it brings. All three rune poems cover it, as ár in the Norse poems and gēr in the Anglo-Saxon; all praise a good year as a gift to people, and the Anglo-Saxon poem adds that its fruits reach rich and poor alike.
ᛇ · sound "ï (between e and i)" · Heimdall's ætt · name means yew tree
endurance, resilience, deep roots, steadiness

The name means yew, a tree that can live for centuries and was prized for making bows. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem covers this rune, praising the yew as rough-barked, firm in the earth and a guardian of fire; the Norse poems also have a yew rune, ýr, but it is a different sign. Its exact sound is uncertain, somewhere between e and i.
ᛈ · sound "p" · Heimdall's ætt · name means uncertain; perhaps a dice cup or a fruit tree
mystery, chance, the unknown, play

No one knows for certain what its name meant; guesses include a dice cup, a gaming piece and a fruit tree. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem covers it, as peorð, and pictures it as play and laughter among companions in the hall, which is why many readers link it with games of chance.
ᛉ · sound "z (later r)" · Heimdall's ætt · name means elk, or protection
protection, awareness, boundaries, shelter

Its name is usually taken to mean elk, or protection. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem gives it a verse of its own, under the name eolhx, the elk-sedge, a marsh grass that cuts the hand of anyone who grabs it. In the later Younger Futhark the same sign, usually turned upside down, kept its sound but took the name ýr, yew, and that is the yew rune the Norse poems describe.
ᛊ · sound "s" · Heimdall's ætt · name means sun
sun, success, vitality, clarity, wholeness

The name means sun. All three rune poems cover it: the Old Norwegian calls the sun the light of the lands, the Old Icelandic a shield in the sky that melts the ice, and the Anglo-Saxon poem, under the name sigel, a hope to sailors until they reach land.
ᛏ · sound "t" · Tyr's ætt · name means the god Tyr
courage, justice, commitment, integrity

The rune is named for Týr, the god who put his hand in the wolf Fenrir's jaws as a pledge so the gods could bind it, and lost the hand. Both Norse poems name it after the one-handed god, while the Anglo-Saxon poem's tīr is a guiding sign that keeps its course through the night, often read as a star.
ᛒ · sound "b" · Tyr's ætt · name means birch
growth, new beginnings, nurture, renewal

The name means birch, one of the first trees to return to open ground. All three rune poems cover it: the Norse verses picture a leafy young twig, while the Anglo-Saxon poem describes a tree that sends up new shoots without seed and stands beautiful in its branches.
ᛖ · sound "e" · Tyr's ætt · name means horse
partnership, trust, progress, teamwork

The name means horse. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem covers it, describing the horse as a joy to nobles, proud of its hooves, and a comfort to anyone who is restless. Horses were companions as much as transport in the early Germanic world, and many readers see that bond in the rune's two linked staves.
ᛗ · sound "m" · Tyr's ætt · name means a human being
humanity, self, community, cooperation

The name means man in the sense of a human being. All three rune poems cover it: the Norse verses call people an increase of the earth, while the Anglo-Saxon poem notes that people are dear to one another and yet must one day part.
ᛚ · sound "l" · Tyr's ætt · name means water, lake
flow, intuition, emotion, what lies beneath

The name is usually reconstructed as water or lake, though some scholars read it as leek, a plant of growth and protection. All three rune poems cover it: the Old Norwegian with a waterfall, the Old Icelandic with an eddying stream, and the Anglo-Saxon with an endless, unsettling sea for those on a tossing ship.
ᛜ · sound "ng" · Tyr's ætt · name means the god Ing
potential, gestation, completion, inner growth

The rune is named for Ing, a god of fertility and plenty linked with Freyr, remembered in later legend as the ancestor of the early Swedish kings. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem covers it, telling how Ing was first seen among the East Danes and later went away over the waves, his wagon following behind.
ᛞ · sound "d" · Tyr's ætt · name means day
daybreak, breakthrough, awakening, hope

The name means day. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem covers it, calling daylight dear to everyone and a source of hope and help to rich and poor alike. Its shape, two halves meeting at a single point, is often read as the balance between night and day.
ᛟ · sound "o" · Tyr's ætt · name means ancestral land, inheritance
home, heritage, belonging, what lasts

The name means inherited land, the family homestead held over generations. Only the Anglo-Saxon poem covers it, as ēþel, describing a home as dear to anyone who can live there as is right and in plenty. In readings it often stands for what a family builds up over time, from land and customs to the stories it tells.
